source.title: Scaling Up Biomedical Vision-Language Models: Fine-Tuning, Instruction Tuning, and Multi-Modal Learning
source.authors: Cheng Peng; Kai Zhang; Mengxian Lyu; Hongfang Liu; Lichao Sun; Yonghui Wu

record.tranche_reason: It measures downstream benchmark performance across model sizes in a different setting from the original scaling-law studies. It tests downstream scaling, but does not fit held-out loss power laws or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream task scores for scaled biomedical vision-language models, which bear on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fit power laws; parameter and data sizes are not varied independently to test loss scaling, and it does not test a compute-optimal allocation. Benchmark comparisons to external models are not evidence about scaling unless they compare the study's own model sizes.
record.test_reason: The study reports downstream scores for its own Base (182M), Large (472M) and XLarge (930M) biomedical vision-language models on 23 fine-tuning and 5 zero-shot datasets. This bears on V6 in a new setting: a multimodal encoder-decoder in the biomedical domain. It is a weak test. There are only three sizes and no curve fit or prediction. Size is confounded: Large and XLarge were also trained on more and longer text (14.5B vs 9.7B words) and initialised from OFA-Large and OFA-Huge. No loss sweeps, power-law fits or allocation experiments appear, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the scaled models beat BiomedGPT-Base on 17 of 23 datasets and reach SOTA on 15 of 23. They credit long-form pretraining text for better long-context use, report that instruction tuning boosts zero-shot performance, and note task-specific dips they call saturation. They also find that continual training from OFA checkpoints beats training from scratch. They do not claim any scaling law or predictable curve.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales an encoder-decoder biomedical vision-language model and evaluates task-specific fine-tuning and instruction-tuned downstream benchmarks. It does not reproduce the original language-model pretraining loss measurements, power-law fits, or compute-allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by task and dataset: the text reports a Large-model dip on MedNLI, MeQSum, and HealthCareMagic, a BloodMNIST dip, and a zero-shot VQA-RAD drop from Large to XLarge. Scores otherwise often rise with size.
record.problems: Only three model sizes are evaluated, with no fitted scaling curve or extrapolation test. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note that automated surface-level metrics may not reflect human evaluation. Model size and training-data changes are not isolated as a single-variable scaling experiment.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was not reached. Other separately reported scaling outcomes from Table 2 and Table 3 are not included here, including additional benchmark datasets and captioning metrics; rows were prioritized to preserve multiple task types and the reported non-monotonic cases. Table 2 also states that single-image MIMIC-CXR CIDEr is an exception to otherwise consistent scaling gains, but the flattened table values do not support a secure assignment of those scores to the individual size checkpoints.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported or fitted against parameters, data or compute.
No small-run fit used to predict larger runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count. Layers and width were both increased together.
Multimodal and fine-tuning settings are used, but no power-law form is fitted in any of them.

Only whether scores rise with size is tested, not predictability. There is no fit to size or pretraining loss and no extrapolation. The size effect is not isolated from added long-form pretraining data and different OFA initialisations.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Single-image captioning size steps. IU X-ray CIDEr 0.401/0.395/0.408 (Large dip). MIMIC-CXR CIDEr 0.262/0.234/0.237 (both larger models below Base; the authors name this as the exception).
missing.locator: Table 2, image captioning; Results paragraph on captioning

missing.what: Multi-image captioning size steps. IU X-ray: GREEN 0.369/0.391/0.463, F1-RadGraph 0.239/0.254/0.288, F1-Chexbert 0.311/0.395/0.412. MIMIC-CXR: GREEN 0.313/0.331/0.343, F1-RadGraph 0.197/0.219/0.257, F1-Chexbert 0.409/0.448/0.520.

Training from scratch vs continual from OFA. From scratch, XLarge underperforms Large on SLAKE (0.740 vs 0.753). Scaling gains are smaller from scratch on PathMNIST (0.946→0.952) and MIMIC-III (0.288→0.305). So the size benefit depends on initialisation.
Zero-shot alignment accuracy and category-level accuracy across sizes on 300 VQA-RAD cases; XLarge is highest.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak V6 test. There are three sizes and no uncertainty estimates, and size is confounded with added pretraining data (9.7B→14.5B words, longer text) and with different OFA initialisations. The table and text disagree in places: the text says Large beat Base on all image datasets, but BloodMNIST drops; the text cites a 3.5% TREC'22 gain that Table 2 does not show. The system is a multimodal encoder-decoder, not a pure language model, so V6 evidence here is out of the claim's original setting.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep against parameter count, token count, or compute.
No small-run loss fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute-budget search over parameter and token allocations.
No comparison of architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates biomedical multimodal tasks and instruction tuning, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in these or other modalities or training regimes.
It measures downstream scores at three model sizes, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss, fit a scaling curve, or establish extrapolation beyond the sizes evaluated.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal split are estimated or compared across fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuned and zero-shot tasks where scores rise Base→Large→XLarge (combined parameter and data scale-up, three points, OFA-initialised)
relationships.reason: Most size steps raise downstream scores, e.g. PEIR GROSS CIDEr 1.227→3.225→3.421 and RSNA zero-shot 0.364→0.532→0.630. Rows r01, r02, r04, r06, r07, r10, r12–r14, r16–r22, r24–r32, r35–r57.
relationships.display_finding: Most size steps improved performance, including PEIR GROSS CIDEr from 1.227 to 3.225 to 3.421 and RSNA zero-shot scores from 0.364 to 0.532 to 0.630.

relationships.condition: Datasets where one size step lowers or barely moves the score (MedNLI, MeQSum, HealthCareMagic, BloodMNIST, zero-shot VQA-RAD; near-flat BreastMNIST, PneumoniaMNIST, TREC'22, zero-shot PathMNIST)
relationships.reason: Improvement with size is not monotonic; the authors call this saturation. Examples: MeQSum 0.523→0.505, zero-shot VQA-RAD 0.519→0.506. Rows r05, r09, r11, r23, r34 drop; r03, r08, r33, r58, r59 are near-flat.
relationships.display_finding: Several tasks plateaued or declined, including MeQSum from 0.523 to 0.505 and zero-shot VQA-RAD from 0.519 to 0.506.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The tested fine-tuned and instruction-tuned datasets with increasing scores as model size grows
reader_labels.reason: The reported downstream scores rise across the compared sizes for these conditions; see rows r01-r04, r06-r08, r10, r12-r19, r20-r22, r24-r29, r30-r33, r35-r43, r44-r57, r58-r59.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MedNLI, MeQSum, HealthCareMagic, BloodMNIST, and instruction-tuned VQA-RAD comparisons where the score falls at one size step
reader_labels.reason: Several downstream scores decline from the smaller to the next larger checkpoint, so increasing performance is not uniform across tested tasks; see rows r05, r09, r11, r23, and r34.
